messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The event that cracked everything open happened three years ago, on a cold November night. Marcus was driving his late shift through the south side, the bus nearly empty, when he saw the flashing lights in his mirror. He pulled over, assuming it was a routine stop—maybe a passenger had complained, or a tail light was out. But the officer who approached was already shouting, hand on his holster, ordering him out of the seat with his hands up. Marcus complied instantly, but the officer shoved him against the side of the bus, wrenched his arms behind his back, and held him there for what felt like an eternity while another officer searched the cabin. It turned out to be a case of mistaken identity—someone had reported a man matching his description, same jacket, same build, driving a similar bus. They let him go with a curt apology, but Marcus never forgot the cold metal of the handcuffs, the officer’s breath hot on his neck, the way his own heart hammered so hard he thought it might stop. He went home that night and sat in the dark for hours, replaying every second.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found himself unable to shake the memory. It would surface without warning—a sudden flash of the officer’s face, the sound of the handcuffs clicking shut—often when he was least prepared, like while he was eating dinner or trying to fall asleep. The more it intruded, the more he began to feel that the world itself had shifted. He had always considered his neighborhood a place of belonging, but now he saw danger in every patrol car, every uniform. He started to believe that people couldn’t be trusted, that the community he had once relied on was just a fragile illusion. These thoughts made him pull away. He stopped attending the weekly block meetings he had helped organize. He stopped greeting his neighbors. When a friend asked him to grab a beer, Marcus made an excuse. He told himself it was safer to be alone.

Driving became a minefield. Every time a police cruiser appeared in his rearview mirror, Marcus’s hands would tighten on the wheel, his jaw clenching. The irritability that followed was hard to contain—he snapped at passengers for minor infractions, once shouting at an elderly woman who took too long to find her fare card. His supervisor noticed the change, warning him about complaints. Marcus knew he was losing control, but the anger felt like the only thing he could hold onto. To manage the rising tension, he started wearing a baseball cap pulled low over his face during his shifts, and he would cover his face with his hands whenever he passed a police station. He also began avoiding people altogether, eating lunch alone in the bus depot rather than the crowded cafeteria. At home, he would blast loud music or the TV until the walls vibrated, trying to drown out the intrusive memories. The distraction worked for a few minutes, but it also made it harder to concentrate on anything else—he found himself zoning out during his favorite shows, unable to follow a plot.

The door-checking started around the same time. Every night, Marcus would get up three or four times to make sure the locks were engaged, running his fingers along the chain, testing the deadbolt. He knew it was irrational, but the ritual gave him a fleeting sense of control. The hypervigilance bled into his sleep, leaving him exhausted. And the exhaustion fed his belief that the world was fundamentally dangerous—after all, if he couldn't even feel safe in his own apartment, what hope was there? This cycle tightened over months. The more he checked doors, the more he saw threats everywhere; the more he saw threats, the more he retreated into isolation; the more isolated he became, the more the intrusive memories returned, sharp and vivid. He started to lose track of why he had once felt connected to anything at all. One afternoon, while driving his route, a police cruiser pulled up alongside him at a red light. Marcus’s heart lurched. He pressed his hand over his mouth, turned up the radio to full volume, and stared straight ahead until the light changed. The memory of that November night washed over him like a wave, and he knew, in that moment, that he could not keep living like this. He called a therapist the next morning, his voice barely above a whisper. What he feared most was that he had already lost the person he used to be—the man who trusted his neighbors, who waved at kids from his bus window, who believed the world was mostly good. He was desperate to find his way back, but he had no idea where to start.
